claims.text: Adding approximately 5 vol% SiC to ZrB2 enables processing at about 1700 °C.
SiC addition during sintering at about 1700 °C triggers in-situ formation of a protective borosilicate phase.
The in-situ borosilicate phase is nanoscale and distributed at grain boundaries and within the ZrB2 matrix.
Possible silicide interphases form in the SiC-modified ZrB2.
The SiC-induced phases refine the ZrB2 grain size.
The SiC-induced phases enhance densification of ZrB2 at about 1700 °C.
During sintering, SiC partially reacts with ZrB2 and available boron to form a liquid-phase borosilicate.
The liquid borosilicate aids densification by filling intergranular spaces.
The borosilicate phase acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress and lowers the oxidation rate.
The borosilicate phase minimizes penetration of liquid plating metals.
Grain refinement produced by liquid-phase sintering increases mechanical strength and structural integrity.
The SiC-modified material will be denser than unmodified ZrB2 processed at about 1700 °C.
The SiC-modified material will have greater mechanical strength than both high-temperature single-phase ZrB2 and lower-temperature unmodified ZrB2.
The SiC-modified material will have superior high-temperature oxidation durability relative to both baselines.
The SiC-modified material will better resist liquid plating-metal corrosion than both baselines.
Conventional single-phase ZrB2 is manufactured at temperatures above 2300 °C.
Lower-temperature processed ZrB2 lacks sufficient oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion resistance.
The proposed material is applicable to high-temperature oxidative environments and molten-metal plating baths.
